To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the number of alien fishes in a community is inversely related to native species richness; and (2) alien fish species tend to feed on low energy yield food items.

(1) the number of established alien fish in a community is inversely proportional to native fish species richness; (2) established alien fish tend to feed on lower trophic levels than native fishes; (3) the trophic traits that favour the establishment of alien fishes are those that allow them to avoid competition and exploitation from native fishes.
native species richness and species level food chain length were important predictors of alien species richness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
elucidating the mechanisms by which native richness and community trophic traits influence the establishment of alien fishes.
the effects of food web structure, species richness and species trophic traits on invasibility.
the role of community and species level trophotrophic traits in predicting the number of alien species.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ability to occupy a niche that is not occupied by native species, and to avoid competition, are the most important factors in the establishment of alien fish species in freshwater systems.
both species richness and trophic traits play a role in determining invasibility.
the biotic resistance hypothesis is scale dependent, and that species traits are also important determinants of invasibility, with trophic level, diet breadth and body size playing important roles.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

native species richness and the exploitation of low energy yield food resources are the main factors that determine the number of alien species that establish in a habitat, and this is reflected in species level trends in the trophic traits.
the biotic interactions between native and alien species are complex and scale dependent.
native richness is a good predictor for the number of alien fishes and that alien species are generally feeding lower down the food chain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the biotic resistance hypothesis, while scale dependent, can still result in observable effects at the community level.
community and species level trophi traits can be used in conjunction with information theoretic analysis to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the invasion process.
the ability to predict establishment of alien species is improved when community level and species level traits are considered in conjunction.
